title: Balanced Search Trees
tagline: AVL rotations, Red-Black trees, and B-trees — the self-balancing structures that keep O(log n) guarantees alive under insertion and deletion.

sections.content:
A plain binary search tree (BST) is one of the most elegant data structures in computer science: every node's left child is smaller, every right child is larger, and search, insert, and delete all run in O(h) where h is the tree's height. That feels great until you notice the fine print — h is not guaranteed to be O(log n). Insert the sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in sorted order and you get a **degenerate BST** that looks exactly like a linked list, with h = n and O(n) operations. This is not a theoretical edge case: real-world data is often nearly sorted (log files, timestamps, auto-incrementing IDs, alphabetical imports), and attackers can craft adversarial insert sequences to deliberately degrade a BST into linear time.

**Balanced search trees** solve this by self-adjusting on every insert and delete to maintain a height that is always O(log n), regardless of input order. The tree does not merely hope to stay balanced — it enforces it with local structural fixes called **rotations** (or node splits, in disk-oriented trees). This chapter builds the complete picture: why balance matters, exactly how the two dominant in-memory structures (AVL trees and Red-Black trees) enforce their invariants, and how B-trees and B+ trees extend the idea to the massive branching factors needed by databases and file systems.

By the end of this chapter you will understand: (1) what makes a BST degenerate and why it matters, (2) the four AVL rotation cases and how to execute them, (3) the five Red-Black invariants and how they bound height at 2 log n, (4) why AVL tends to be slightly faster for reads while Red-Black does less work on writes, (5) how B-trees pack hundreds of keys per node to minimise disk I/O, and (6) how B+ trees add linked leaves to enable efficient range queries — the index structure that powers every relational database you have ever used.

sections.caption: The core problem: sorted insertion degenerates a BST to a linked list. Balanced search trees prevent this regardless of input order.

sections.title: The Self-Levelling Shelf
sections.content:
Imagine a very long bookshelf divided into two sides. Each time you add a book you must put it on the left side if it comes alphabetically before the centre book, or on the right side if it comes after. This works great when books arrive in random order — both sides stay roughly even. But if you add books A, B, C, D, E, F in order, every book ends up on the right side of the previous one and your 'shelf' becomes a single leaning tower.

A balanced search tree is like having a tidy librarian who, after you place each book, steps back, inspects the shelf, and makes at most one or two small **swaps** — moving a book up or down — to keep both sides roughly equal in length. The swaps are so local and fast (O(1) pointer changes) that the total overhead per operation is still O(log n).

The librarian's rulebook differs by tree type. An AVL librarian is a perfectionist: the two sides may differ in height by at most one book. A Red-Black librarian is more relaxed: she paints books either red or black, and as long as every path from top to bottom has the same number of black books — and no two red books sit adjacent — she is happy. A B-tree librarian manages an enormous warehouse with very wide shelves: instead of swapping books, she splits a full shelf into two when it overflows, keeping all shelves at exactly the same depth from the ground.

sections.title: Why Height Is Everything: The Degenerate BST Problem
sections.content:
Before diving into solutions, it is worth making the degenerate BST problem concrete. A BST with n nodes has height h somewhere between ⌊log₂ n⌋ (perfect binary tree — best case) and n − 1 (linear chain — worst case). Every operation — search, insert, delete — traverses from root to a leaf, so its cost is O(h).

For a random permutation of n distinct keys, the expected height of a BST is about 4.311 ln n, which is O(log n). So random insertion is fine. The danger is **structured input**: sorted ascending, sorted descending, alternating extremes, or any other pattern that consistently sends new nodes to one side. Given that auto-increment primary keys, timestamped events, alphabetical imports, and similar patterns are common in production, relying on 'probably random' is reckless.

Worst-case structure is also an attack surface: the 2011 hash-flooding attacks against PHP, Java, and Ruby web servers worked by forcing O(n) behaviour out of a structure whose *average* case was fine. Any unbalanced structure fed with attacker-controlled keys has the same weakness. **Self-balancing is not a micro-optimisation — it turns an average-case hope into a worst-case guarantee.**

The key insight that makes balancing tractable is that you never need to rebuild the entire tree. A **rotation** — a local rewiring of three nodes and a few pointers — can reduce height imbalance by one while preserving the BST ordering property exactly. Compose a small number of rotations after each insert or delete, and you can maintain O(log n) height forever.

sections.caption: Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in sorted order into a plain BST: a right-skewed chain with 5 levels (height 4 counting edges). Every search for the largest key traverses all 5 nodes — O(n).

sections.title: AVL Trees: Strict Balance via Rotation
sections.content:
AVL trees were invented by Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis in 1962 — the first self-balancing BST ever published. Their key idea: attach a **balance factor** to every node, defined as `height(left subtree) − height(right subtree)`. A valid AVL node must have a balance factor of −1, 0, or +1. Any deviation — a balance factor of ±2 — triggers a rebalancing rotation.

**Computing height:** Each node stores its height explicitly (an integer). The height of a null node is 0 (or −1, depending on convention — just be consistent). After any structural change, you recompute heights bottom-up along the path from the modified node to the root. This is O(log n) total.

**The four imbalance cases** each correspond to a distinct rotation or double rotation:

**Case 1 — Left-Left (LL):** The imbalanced node `z` is left-heavy (balance factor +2), and its left child `y` is also left-heavy or neutral (balance factor ≥ 0). The new node was inserted into `y`'s left subtree. Fix: a single **right rotation** on `z`. `y` becomes the new subtree root, `z` drops to `y`'s right child, and `y`'s old right subtree `T2` becomes `z`'s left child. BST order is preserved because all keys in `T2` are between `y` and `z`.

**Case 2 — Right-Right (RR):** Mirror of LL. `z` is right-heavy, `y` is its right child. Fix: single **left rotation** on `z`.

**Case 3 — Left-Right (LR):** `z` is left-heavy, but `y` (its left child) is right-heavy (balance factor −1). The new node was inserted into `y`'s right subtree. A single right rotation on `z` would not fix this. Fix: first rotate **left on `y`** (converting LR to LL), then rotate **right on `z`**. Two rotations total.

**Case 4 — Right-Left (RL):** Mirror of LR. Fix: rotate right on `z`'s right child, then rotate left on `z`.

After rebalancing, the height of the subtree that was previously imbalanced is the same as before the insert — so the fix never propagates further up the tree for insertion. For deletion, however, height can decrease, which may trigger more rotations up to the root: O(log n) rotations in the worst case for deletion.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The crucial pattern is that `#insert` returns the (possibly new) subtree root after calling `#balance`. This 'returning up the recursion stack' is how height fixes propagate. `#balance` unifies all four cases: it checks whether we have a double rotation (LR or RL) by examining the child's balance factor before applying the outer rotation. After inserting 7 sorted keys a plain BST would have height 7; the AVL tree caps it at 3.

sections.title: Red-Black Trees: Relaxed Balance via Colour Invariants
sections.content:
Red-Black trees were introduced by Rudolf Bayer in 1972 (as 'symmetric binary B-trees') and refined by Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978. They relax the strict AVL balance requirement in exchange for far fewer rotations per write operation — making them the preferred choice for general-purpose sorted maps in standard libraries.

**The five Red-Black invariants** (every valid Red-Black tree satisfies all five simultaneously):
1. Every node is either **red** or **black**.
2. The **root** is black.
3. Every **null leaf** (sentinel) is black.
4. If a node is **red**, both its children are **black** (no two consecutive red nodes).
5. Every path from a given node down to any null leaf passes through the **same number of black nodes** — this number is called the **black-height** of that node.

These invariants together guarantee that the longest root-to-leaf path is at most **twice** the shortest path. The shortest path contains only black nodes (length = black-height `bh`). The longest path alternates red and black nodes (length = 2 × bh). Since a binary tree with all paths of length at least bh has at least 2^bh − 1 internal nodes, we get bh ≤ log₂(n+1), and thus height ≤ 2 log₂(n+1). That worst-case bound is about 1.39× AVL's 1.44 log₂ n bound, but the difference in absolute height for any realistic n is small (for n = 1,000,000: AVL ≤ ~29 levels, Red-Black ≤ ~40), and in practice both trees usually sit much closer to log₂ n ≈ 20.

**Rebalancing after insert:** The new node is always inserted red (to preserve black-height). If its parent is black, done. If its parent is red, we have two consecutive reds — an invariant violation. The fix depends on the colour of the 'uncle' node (the sibling of the parent):
- **Uncle is red:** Recolour parent and uncle to black, grandparent to red. Push the potential violation up to the grandparent. This may propagate up to O(log n) recolourings, but at most 2 rotations total.
- **Uncle is black:** Apply one or two rotations, recolour — and the violation is fully resolved in O(1) additional steps. At most 2 rotations per insert.

**Rebalancing after delete:** Deletion can create a 'double black' node — a node that accounts for two units of black on some paths. Resolving double black requires examining the sibling's colour and its children's colours, and applying up to 3 rotations total. The analysis is more complex but the bound is tight.

sections.title: AVL vs Red-Black: When to Choose Which
sections.content:
Both AVL trees and Red-Black trees provide O(log n) search, insert, and delete. The practical difference lies in **constant factors and rotation counts** — not Big-O complexity class.

**Height comparison for n = 1,000,000 nodes:**
- Perfect BST (theoretical best): height ≈ 20
- AVL tree: height ≤ 1.44 × log₂(n) ≈ 29
- Red-Black tree: height ≤ 2 × log₂(n+1) ≈ 40

AVL's stricter invariant produces a shorter, flatter tree. A shorter tree means fewer node comparisons per search, so AVL lookups are typically a little faster. That makes AVL a reasonable choice for **read-heavy, in-memory** workloads with few updates.

**Rotation counts per operation:**
- AVL insert: at most 2 rotations (one double rotation at the lowest imbalance point).
- AVL delete: up to O(log n) rotations, potentially all the way to the root.
- Red-Black insert: at most 2 rotations, plus O(log n) recolourings (cheap).
- Red-Black delete: at most 3 rotations total.

The bounded rotation count — and fewer rebalancing steps in general — makes Red-Black trees a good default for **mixed and write-heavy** workloads. This is why Java's `TreeMap` and `TreeSet`, C++'s `std::map` and `std::set` (in all major implementations), and the Linux kernel's scheduler run queue (CFS, and its successor EEVDF since Linux 6.6) all use Red-Black trees. In practice the measured difference between AVL and Red-Black is modest and workload-dependent.

**A useful heuristic for interviews and system design:** If you need an ordered map and reads dominate, AVL is theoretically better. If writes (inserts and deletes) are frequent or balanced with reads, use Red-Black (which is what your language's standard library almost certainly provides). For disk-based storage, neither — use B-trees.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The invariant checker walks the tree once, verifying the colour rules and computing the black-height at each node. The recursive structure mirrors how the actual rebalancing code propagates information: every call returns the black-height of its subtree, and mismatches surface the exact location of the violation. This pattern is the basis for every RB-tree test suite.

sections.title: B-Trees: Balancing on Disk
sections.content:
AVL and Red-Black trees are elegant for **in-memory** data. But databases and file systems operate on **disk**, where the rules are completely different. A single spinning-disk seek takes roughly 5–10 milliseconds — on the order of 100,000× slower than a ~100 ns RAM access; even an NVMe SSD random read (~10–100 µs) is 100–1,000× slower than RAM. An operation that performs 30 node reads from a binary tree (as O(log₂ n) requires for n = 1 billion) incurs 30 random reads, which at 10 ms each means 300 ms — about a third of a second for one lookup. This is completely unacceptable for a database index.

The solution is to change the **branching factor**. Instead of each node having at most 2 children, let each node have up to **M** children. A **B-tree of order M** satisfies:
- Every node holds at most **M − 1 keys** and **M child pointers**.
- Every non-root node holds at least **⌈M/2⌉ − 1 keys**.
- The **root** holds at least 1 key (or is a leaf).
- All **leaves are at the same depth** — B-trees are perfectly height-balanced.
- Keys within a node are sorted; child pointers separate consecutive key ranges.

With a disk page of 4 KB and keys of 8 bytes plus pointers of 8 bytes, you can fit roughly **M = 200** entries per node (real databases use 8–16 KB pages and fit several hundred). A 4-level B-tree has 200³ ≈ 8 million nodes at the bottom level, each holding ~200 keys, so it can index **≈ 1.6 billion keys (≈ 200⁴)** while reading at most **4 pages** per lookup — and the top two levels are almost always cached in RAM. A binary tree over the same keys would need ⌈log₂(1.6 × 10⁹)⌉ = 31 reads. The branching factor is the entire game.

**B-tree insert:** Insert the key into the correct leaf. If the leaf overflows (more than M − 1 keys), **split** it: push the median key up to the parent and create a new sibling node. The split may propagate up if the parent also overflows. In the worst case, a chain of splits reaches the root, increasing tree height by one — the only way a B-tree grows taller.

**B-tree delete:** Find and remove the key. If the node becomes under-full (fewer than ⌈M/2⌉ − 1 keys), try to **borrow** a key from an adjacent sibling through the parent. If the sibling is also too small, **merge** the node, sibling, and the separating parent key into one node, then repeat up the tree. This is the mirror of insertion.

**Height bound:** A B-tree with n keys has height at most log_{⌈M/2⌉}((n+1)/2). For M = 200, this is log₁₀₀(n/2). For n = 1 billion: log₁₀₀(500,000,000) ≈ 4.4 — so about 5 levels. Five disk reads to find any record among a billion.

sections.title: B+ Trees: Range Queries and the Linked Leaf Layer
sections.content:
Every major relational database — PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, SQLite — uses a **B+ tree** variant rather than a plain B-tree. The difference is subtle but enormously impactful for query performance.

**In a plain B-tree**, both internal nodes and leaf nodes store actual record data (or pointers to records). A range query such as `age BETWEEN 25 AND 40` is still possible — an in-order traversal from the first match — but the traversal has to bounce up and down between leaves and internal nodes (keeping a stack of ancestors), re-reading internal pages along the way. There is no direct link from one leaf to the next.

**In a B+ tree:**
- **Internal nodes** store only **keys** (no record data). This allows them to hold more keys, increasing the branching factor and further reducing height.
- **Leaf nodes** store all the actual records (or record pointers) and are connected as a **doubly-linked list** sorted by key.
- Every key that appears in an internal node also appears in a leaf (as a duplicate copy).

This architecture makes **range queries** extremely efficient. To find all employees aged 25–40:
1. Traverse from root to the leaf containing key 25 — O(log n) disk reads.
2. Walk the linked list of leaves rightward until you pass key 40 — O(k/L) reads where k is the number of qualifying records and L is the leaf capacity.

Asymptotically a careful B-tree in-order scan is also O(log n + k/L) page visits, but its access pattern jumps between levels, while a B+ tree scan is a straight sequential walk along the leaf chain — friendlier to caches, read-ahead, and concurrent access. Combined with the higher fan-out of key-only internal nodes, that is why B+ trees won.

**Why internal nodes store only keys:** A 4KB page holding only 8-byte keys plus pointers fits about 250 entries. A page holding full records (say, 100 bytes each) fits only about 40. The larger branching factor means fewer levels, fewer disk reads per lookup. Everything in database indexing comes back to minimising disk I/O.

**Real-world indexes:** PostgreSQL's default index type is B-tree (which in practice is B+ tree). MySQL InnoDB uses a clustered B+ tree where the primary key index IS the table — the leaves contain the full row data. Secondary indexes store the primary key rather than a physical row address, so rows can move between pages (on splits and merges) without updating every secondary index — at the cost of a second lookup through the primary index. SQLite likewise uses B+ trees for both indexes and table storage.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `findStartLeaf` function simulates the O(log n) traversal from root to the first qualifying leaf. The `rangeQuery` function then walks the linked list in O(k) time, collecting results until it passes the upper bound. In a real B+ tree with millions of records and disk pages, the sequential leaf walk avoids re-visiting internal pages for every few results, which is what an in-order scan of a plain B-tree has to do.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Misconception 1: 'Balanced' means all subtrees are the same height.** AVL trees allow a height difference of 1 at every node — not zero. Red-Black trees allow the longest path to be twice the shortest. 'Balanced' in the context of search trees means 'height is O(log n)', not 'perfectly symmetric'. A perfectly balanced tree would be too expensive to maintain.

**Misconception 2: You must implement AVL/RB from scratch in interviews.** Almost never. What interviewers actually care about is: (a) can you recognise when a problem needs a sorted dynamic structure, (b) do you know the O(log n) complexity guarantees, and (c) can you describe why plain BST is insufficient. Implementing rotations from scratch is typically reserved for systems programming or OS courses. Knowing the interface and properties is sufficient for 95% of software engineering interviews.

**Misconception 3: B-tree equals B+ tree.** They are related but different. A plain B-tree stores data in both internal and leaf nodes. A B+ tree stores data ONLY in leaves, with internal nodes acting as a pure routing layer. Almost all production databases use B+ trees specifically for the linked-leaf range query advantage.

**Edge case: Duplicate keys.** Neither AVL nor Red-Black trees as traditionally defined handle duplicate keys. Common solutions: store a count at each node, store a list at each node, or define that duplicates go left (or right) consistently. B-trees for databases use composite keys (data + primary key) to make all keys unique.

**Edge case: Empty tree operations.** Both search and rotation code must handle null/empty nodes explicitly. A common bug is forgetting that a 'null node has height 0' when computing balance factors — the height of a null child must return 0 (or −1, depending on convention), not cause a null dereference.

**Edge case: Single-node AVL tree.** A single node has balance factor 0 and is perfectly balanced by definition. The height is 1. No rotation is ever needed until a second node is inserted.

sections.title: Real-World Relevance: Where Balanced Trees Appear in Production
sections.content:
Balanced search trees are not textbook curiosities — they are the backbone of production systems you interact with every day.

**Operating system schedulers:** The Linux kernel keeps runnable tasks in a Red-Black tree. Under the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS, 2007–2023) the leftmost node (smallest virtual runtime) runs next; its successor EEVDF (default since Linux 6.6) still uses an augmented Red-Black tree to pick the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline. Inserts and deletes happen on every context switch, so O(log n) with bounded rotations matters.

**Standard library sorted maps:** Java's `TreeMap` and `TreeSet` (Red-Black), C++'s `std::map` and `std::set` (Red-Black), and Rust's `BTreeMap` (a B-tree variant) all implement ordered maps with O(log n) operations. These are the go-to structures when you need sorted iteration plus efficient point lookup.

**Database indexes:** PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQLite, Oracle, and SQL Server all use B+ trees as their default index structure. Every `CREATE INDEX` you execute creates a B+ tree on disk. The WHERE clause of a SELECT query navigates this B+ tree to avoid full table scans.

**File systems:** NTFS (Windows) uses B+ trees to store file metadata. HFS+ and APFS (macOS) use B-trees. The ext4 filesystem uses an extent tree (a B-tree variant) for managing file block extents.

**In-memory key-value stores:** Redis sorted sets are implemented as a skip list (a probabilistic alternative to balanced BSTs) plus a hash table. Redis's author chose skip lists over balanced trees because they are simpler to implement, easy to augment for rank queries (`ZRANK`), and make range scans straightforward. Skip lists also back the memtables of LevelDB and RocksDB.

Understanding balanced trees unlocks your ability to reason about the performance of all these systems — not just how to use them, but why they perform the way they do under load.

**B+ trees are not the only disk index.** Write-heavy stores — RocksDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, LevelDB, and many time-series databases — use **LSM-trees** (log-structured merge trees): writes go to an in-memory sorted structure (often a skip list), which is flushed to immutable sorted files (SSTables) and merged in the background. LSM-trees turn random writes into sequential ones at the cost of read amplification (a lookup may check several files, mitigated by per-file Bloom filters). Rule of thumb: B+ tree for read-heavy OLTP with in-place updates; LSM-tree for very high write throughput.

**A brief history:** AVL trees (1962) predate the microprocessor. Adelson-Velsky and Landis published their paper in Russian; it was years before Western computer scientists fully absorbed it. Red-Black trees emerged from Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-trees and were given their colour terminology by Guibas and Sedgewick in 1978. B-trees were invented by Bayer and McCreight at Boeing Research Labs in 1970, specifically for disk-based storage — the paper title was 'Organization and Maintenance of Large Ordered Indices.' The fact that structures designed in 1962 and 1970 are still the default index structures in PostgreSQL and Linux in 2026 speaks to how fundamentally correct the underlying ideas are.

**Interview and system design guide:** (1) If asked 'what data structure for a sorted dynamic set with O(log n) operations?' — say balanced BST, specifically Red-Black or AVL. (2) If the interviewer asks which one — say Red-Black for write-heavy (standard library default), AVL for read-heavy. (3) If the system design question involves a database index or file system — always say B+ tree and explain the linked-leaf layer for range scans. (4) In JavaScript/Python, reach for a sorted array with binary search for small n (simpler); for large n with frequent modifications, use a library-provided sorted map or describe the B+ tree you would use. (5) The most common rotation mistake: forgetting to update heights AFTER reassigning children — update the lower node first, then the new root, or your heights will be wrong.

items: A plain BST degenerates to O(n) height on sorted input — a common real-world case. Balanced search trees enforce O(log n) height by self-adjusting via rotations or node splits after every modification.

AVL trees maintain a strict balance factor (|left_h − right_h| ≤ 1) at every node, guaranteeing height ≤ 1.44 log₂ n. Four rotation cases (LL, RR, LR, RL) restore balance after each insert; inserts need at most 2 rotations but deletes may need O(log n).

Red-Black trees use five colour invariants — equal black-height on every root-to-null path, no consecutive red nodes — bounding height at 2 log₂(n+1). Inserts need at most 2 rotations; deletes need at most 3. This makes Red-Black the choice for write-heavy workloads and all major standard library sorted maps.

B-trees generalise BSTs to nodes with up to M children. A single node fits one disk page; with M ≈ 200, a 4-level B-tree indexes ~1.6 billion keys (≈ 200⁴) with only 4 page reads. All leaves remain at the same depth, maintained by splitting full nodes on insert and merging under-full nodes on delete.

B+ trees store all records exclusively in leaf nodes, with internal nodes acting as a pure routing layer holding more keys. Leaves are connected as a doubly-linked list, enabling O(log n + k) range queries — the reason every major relational database uses B+ trees as its default index structure.

The key practical tradeoff is AVL (shorter tree, faster reads) vs Red-Black (bounded write rotations, standard library default) vs B+ tree (disk-oriented, database indexes). The Big-O class is the same for all; the difference is in constant factors, rotation counts, and I/O patterns.

Balanced trees are deployed at scale in the Linux scheduler (Red-Black, CFS and now EEVDF), Java TreeMap / C++ std::map (Red-Black), Rust BTreeMap (B-tree), PostgreSQL/MySQL indexes (B+ tree), and NTFS/APFS/ext4 file systems (B-tree variants). Write-heavy stores often use LSM-trees instead of B+ trees. Understanding the invariants explains their performance characteristics in production.

quiz.question: Inserting the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order into a plain BST produces a tree with how many levels (nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path)?
options: 3 (like a balanced tree)
5 (degenerate chain — one node per level)
2 (perfectly balanced)
quiz.explanation: Sorted insertion always sends each new key to the rightmost position, creating a right-skewed chain. For n=5 keys, the chain has 5 levels (height 4 if you count edges). Every operation on this degenerate tree costs O(n), not O(log n).

quiz.question: What is the balance factor of an AVL node, and what values are permitted?
options: The height of the left subtree minus the height of the right subtree; must be -1, 0, or +1
The ratio of left to right subtree sizes; must equal 1.0
The number of nodes in the left subtree minus the right; must be within 10% of each other
The colour of the node (red or black); must alternate with parent
quiz.explanation: The AVL balance factor at a node is height(left) - height(right). A valid AVL tree requires this to be -1, 0, or +1 at every node. A value of ±2 indicates imbalance and triggers a rotation.

quiz.question: Which rotation sequence fixes the Left-Right (LR) imbalance case in an AVL tree?
options: A single right rotation on the imbalanced node
A single left rotation on the imbalanced node
A left rotation on the left child, then a right rotation on the imbalanced node
A right rotation on the right child, then a left rotation on the imbalanced node
quiz.explanation: The LR case: the imbalanced node z is left-heavy, but its left child y is right-heavy. A single right rotation on z would not fix it. Instead: first rotate left on y (converting LR to LL), then rotate right on z. This is always exactly two rotations for the LR case.

quiz.question: What is the maximum height of a Red-Black tree with n nodes?
options: log₂(n)
1.44 × log₂(n)
2 × log₂(n+1)
quiz.explanation: The Red-Black invariants (equal black-height on all root-to-null paths; no two consecutive red nodes) mean the longest path alternates red and black, so its length is at most 2 × the shortest path. The shortest path length is the black-height bh ≥ ½ × height, giving height ≤ 2 × log₂(n+1). AVL's bound is tighter at 1.44 × log₂(n).

quiz.question: Why are Red-Black trees preferred over AVL trees in most standard library sorted maps (Java TreeMap, C++ std::map)?
options: Red-Black trees support duplicate keys natively, while AVL trees cannot
Red-Black trees require at most 3 rotations per delete vs AVL's O(log n), making writes faster
Red-Black trees produce a shorter tree, so searches are faster
Red-Black trees do not require rebalancing after insertion
quiz.explanation: AVL's stricter balance means deletion may propagate rotations all the way to the root — O(log n) rotations. Red-Black trees cap deletes at 3 rotations (plus O(log n) cheap recolourings). For general-purpose sorted maps where inserts and deletes are common, this constant bound on rotations makes Red-Black consistently faster on writes.

quiz.question: In a B-tree of order M, what happens when a node overflows during an insert?
options: The tree rebalances via rotations like an AVL tree
The tree height doubles to accommodate the new key
The excess key is discarded and re-inserted into the root
The node is split: its median key is pushed up to the parent, and a new sibling node is created
quiz.explanation: When a B-tree node accumulates more than M-1 keys, it splits: the median key is promoted to the parent, and the node's keys are divided between the original node and a new sibling. This may cascade to the parent if it also overflows. The only way a B-tree grows taller is if the root itself splits.

quiz.question: A B-tree with branching factor M=200 has height 4. Approximately how many records can it index?
options: 1.6 billion (200⁴)
quiz.explanation: With 4 levels and fan-out 200, the bottom level has about 200³ = 8 million nodes, each holding roughly 200 keys — about 200⁴ ≈ 1.6 billion keys in total. This is why databases with billions of records still achieve lookups in 4-5 disk reads.

quiz.question: What structural feature of B+ trees makes range queries (e.g., 'find all rows where age BETWEEN 25 AND 40') much faster than in plain B-trees?
options: B+ trees store all records in internal nodes for faster access
B+ trees use hash buckets at each leaf for O(1) lookup within a page
B+ tree leaves are connected as a doubly-linked list, so after finding the first matching key with O(log n) traversal, the rest of the range is a linear leaf scan
B+ trees duplicate keys across multiple leaves to allow parallel range scans
quiz.explanation: In a B+ tree, all records live in leaf nodes and leaves are linked sequentially. A range query navigates from the root to the first qualifying leaf in O(log n) disk reads, then walks the linked list to collect all results in O(k/L) additional reads where k is the result count and L is the leaf capacity. In a plain B-tree, data lives in internal nodes too, so an in-order scan must keep climbing back into internal nodes instead of walking a simple chain of leaves.

quiz.question: Which of these systems uses a Red-Black tree in its implementation?
options: The Linux kernel scheduler's run queue (CFS, and EEVDF since Linux 6.6)
PostgreSQL's default index (B+ tree on disk)
JavaScript's built-in Map object (hash table)
MySQL InnoDB's primary key index (clustered B+ tree)
quiz.explanation: The Linux scheduler stores runnable tasks in a Red-Black tree — keyed by virtual runtime under CFS (the leftmost node runs next), and as an augmented tree ordered by virtual deadline under EEVDF. Insert and delete happen on every context switch, so bounded rotations and O(log n) per operation are essential. PostgreSQL and MySQL use B+ trees; JS Map is a hash table.

quiz.question: After inserting a new red node into a Red-Black tree, the node's parent is also red (violating invariant 4). The uncle node is RED. What is the correct fix?
options: Perform a rotation at the grandparent to restore balance immediately
Recolour the parent and uncle to black and the grandparent to red, then check the grandparent's parent for violations
Recolour only the new node to black to eliminate the consecutive reds
Split the grandparent node as in a B-tree insertion
quiz.explanation: When the uncle is RED, no rotation is needed yet. Recolour parent and uncle to black, and grandparent to red. This fixes the local violation but may push a red-red conflict up to the grandparent. The algorithm then checks the grandparent's parent, propagating up to O(log n) recolourings. At most 2 rotations occur during the entire insert, only when an uncle is BLACK.
